weekLabel: Week 9 · Meeting A · Parameter Sweeps and Sensitivity

slides.title: Which lever actually moves the number?
slides.subtitle: Parameter sweeps and sensitivity on Radley Hall's south wing — window-to-wall ratio vs. shading depth, and the NumPy tools that answer it
slides.teaching: Open with the question, not the vocabulary: Radley Hall's new south wing has two design knobs on the table — window-to-wall ratio and shading depth. Ask the room to guess, right now, which one they'd change first if told to cut energy use. Do not answer yet — today builds the tool that actually answers it.

slides.title: A sweep answers what one run cannot
slides.statement: Running a performance formula once tells you one design's score. Running it across every plausible value of two design variables tells you which one actually moves that score.
slides.supporting: Today's fictional scoring formula, energy_proxy, takes a window-to-wall ratio (wwr) and a shading overhang depth (shade_m) and returns one number to MINIMIZE — an energy-use-intensity-like proxy. You do not derive this formula; it is provided, exactly like Radley Hall's other data.
slides.teaching: Preview that 'minimize' is doing real work here — lower is better. Do not yet name scipy.optimize.minimize; that is Week 11. Today the method is exhaustive: try many values and read the result.

slides.title: Sensitivity, defined

left.head: One input at a time
left.body: Sensitivity: how much an outcome changes when you change one input. A design variable is 'high sensitivity' if a small change swings the result a lot, and 'low sensitivity' if the result barely moves.

right.head: With two inputs, together
right.body: A sensitivity ANALYSIS compares two or more inputs' effects side by side to find which one moves the outcome the most — exactly today's question: does wwr or shade_m move energy_proxy more?

slides.teaching: Say this word plainly before it appears again on every later slide: sensitivity is not a NumPy term, it is the design question itself — the NumPy tools that follow exist only to answer it.

outcomes.head: Pose
outcomes.body: State a two-variable sensitivity question before writing any NumPy syntax: which input moves the outcome most?

outcomes.head: Sweep
outcomes.body: Use arange/linspace to generate many evenly spaced design values, and call a formula on the whole ndarray at once instead of one value at a time.

outcomes.head: Combine
outcomes.body: Use meshgrid to evaluate every combination of two swept variables together, not just one variable at a time.

outcomes.head: Read
outcomes.body: Use a boolean mask to flag which combinations meet a target, and read a swept surface to state which region performs best.

slides.teaching: Flag outcome 1 explicitly as the one this deck protects hardest — the question must exist before any tool is named.

items: State the question: wwr vs. shade_m, which moves energy_proxy most?
One variable at a time -- and a trap hiding in that approach
Boolean mask: flag combinations that meet a target
meshgrid: sweep both variables together, then read the surface
slides.teaching: Tell students the trap in item 2 is not a throwaway aside — it is the reason meshgrid exists, and the exact reasoning returns in Week 11 when a single starting guess plays the same role a single fixed baseline plays today.

slides.title: Today's design problem, stated plainly

left.head: Two design variables
left.body:
wwr — window-to-wall ratio, bounded 0.20 to 0.60 (fraction of exterior wall that is glazing).
shade_m — overhang depth in meters, bounded 0.0 to 1.2.
Both describe Radley Hall's new south wing (fictional, like every other Radley Hall number this semester).

right.head: One score to minimize
right.body: energy_proxy(wwr, shade_m) returns a single fictional energy-use-intensity-like number. Lower is better. It is a provided formula — you will call it, sweep it, and visualize it, the same way Week 4 called a provided course_style function without editing it.

slides.teaching: Write both bounds on the board before any code appears. Emphasize 'provided' — no one is expected to derive a two-basin formula by hand; the skill this week is calling and sweeping it, not deriving it.

slides.title: The provided formula — start with one Gaussian dip
slides.code:
import numpy as np

def basin(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, cx: float,
          cy: float, depth: float, wx: float,
          wy: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Gaussian dip of depth, centered at (cx, cy)."""
    dx = ((x - cx) ** 2) / (2 * wx ** 2)
    dy = ((y - cy) ** 2) / (2 * wy ** 2)
    return -depth * np.exp(-(dx + dy))

print(round(basin(0.40, 0.30, 0.52, 0.25,
                  30.0, 0.06, 0.18), 3))
slides.explainHead: A dip is deepest at its own center
slides.explainBody: basin is the single helper the whole formula is built from: a smooth dip reaching its lowest value, -depth, exactly at (cx, cy) and fading back toward 0 as you move away. The docstring and type hints are this course's convention from Week 4 onward — every function you define gets both, so a reader knows what goes in and what comes back without running it. At the baseline design (0.40, 0.30), a dip centered at (0.52, 0.25) contributes only -3.906.
slides.teaching: Do not derive this shape — say plainly 'it is provided, like Radley Hall's other numbers.' The one fact worth naming out loud: the value is most negative at the dip's own center and approaches 0 far from it, so landing near a deep dip is exactly what makes a design score well.

slides.title: ...continued: two dips and a ridge become energy_proxy
slides.code:
def energy_proxy(v: tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    """Provided proxy to MINIMIZE; v=(wwr, shade_m)."""
    w, s = v
    base = 20.0
    b1 = basin(w, s, 0.52, 0.25, 30.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    b2 = basin(w, s, 0.28, 0.90, 34.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    ridge = 6.0 * np.exp(-((w - 0.40) ** 2) / 0.02)
    return base + b1 + b2 + ridge

baseline = energy_proxy((0.40, 0.30))
print(f'{baseline:.3f}')
slides.explainHead: One call, one number, one design
slides.explainBody: energy_proxy takes its two variables packed into one input v = (wwr, shade_m) — unpacked inside as w, s. That exact shape is deliberate: Week 11 hands this identical function to scipy.optimize.minimize, which expects a formula written exactly this way. Two basin calls place the two dips; ridge adds a soft wall near wwr=0.40. Today, just call it: a 0.40 wwr, 0.30 m overhang baseline design scores 22.076.
slides.teaching: Trace each of the three named pieces — b1, b2, ridge — back to the previous slide's basin call, then say plainly 'lower is better, and this baseline is not yet the answer to anything.' Verified against real numpy 2.4.6.

slides.title: The question
slides.statement: Which of wwr and shade_m moves energy_proxy the most — and how would you find out without typing this exact call a hundred times by hand?
slides.supporting: That second half of the question is what today's NumPy tools exist to answer. Every tool introduced from here on is in service of answering it faster and more completely than typing one call at a time.
slides.teaching: Pause here. This is the pivot slide — confirm out loud that no NumPy vocabulary has been used as a goal in itself yet, only as needed to answer this exact, already-posed question.

slides.title: ndarray, defined
slides.definition: NumPy's core array type. Arithmetic and a function call apply to EVERY element of an ndarray at once (vectorization) — no explicit loop required. A plain Python list has no idea its elements are numbers to compute with together; an ndarray does.

example.head: np.array([0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60])
example.body: Looks exactly like a list literal — but energy_proxy((wwr_demo, 0.30)) runs the whole formula on all five values at once. The next few slides formalize this behavior as 'vectorization.'

slides.note: np.array([...]) is built FROM a list, but once built it is a different type entirely: list + list concatenates two lists end to end; ndarray + ndarray adds element by element.
slides.teaching: Draw the contrast concretely: a list is a shelf of boxes you open one at a time; an ndarray is a shelf you can restock all at once. The next two slides make this literal with the same five numbers, two ways.

slides.title: One value at a time — five typed calls
slides.explainHead: This works — and does not scale
slides.explainBody: Five values, five typed lines, five separate calls. Sweeping 41 values this way means 41 lines, or a loop nobody wants to hand-verify. Every value is still computed correctly — the problem is effort and clarity, not correctness.
slides.teaching: Ask: what would this loop look like for 81 wwr values crossed with 61 shade values — 4,941 lines? That number returns explicitly a few slides from now.

slides.title: The same five numbers, one vectorized call
slides.code:
import numpy as np

wwr_demo = np.array([0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60])
scores = energy_proxy((wwr_demo, 0.30))
print(np.round(scores, 3))
slides.explainHead: Same formula, same five answers, one line
slides.explainBody: wwr_demo is an ndarray, not a list. energy_proxy((wwr_demo, 0.30)) runs the entire formula on all five values at once — no for loop, no accumulator. Every number matches the loop version exactly, because it is the identical arithmetic, just applied to every element together.
slides.teaching: Have students eyeball-match this array against the previous slide's five printed lines — same numbers, same order, radically less code.

slides.title: Vectorization, defined
slides.definition: Applying one operation to an entire ndarray at once, so NumPy's own fast internal loop replaces an explicit Python for loop. The math does not change — only how many lines of code it takes to run it.

example.head: energy_proxy((wwr_demo, 0.30))
example.body: The for loop two slides ago and this one-line call compute the identical five numbers. Only this one is vectorized: no loop, no accumulator — and every sweep for the rest of this deck depends on that.

slides.note: A sweep of 4,941 combinations later in this deck would mean 4,941 typed lines without vectorization — not just slower to run, unreasonable to even type.
slides.teaching: Name the word out loud now that both versions have been seen side by side — vectorization is the property, ndarray is the type that makes it possible.

slides.title: np.arange, defined
slides.definition: np.arange(start, stop, step) builds evenly spaced values by STEP SIZE. The stop value is EXCLUDED — the last value generated is the largest one strictly less than stop.

example.head: np.arange(0.20, 0.60, 0.05)
example.body: Gives 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, ... up to (not including) 0.60 — 8 values, not 9, because 0.60 itself is excluded.

slides.note: Floating-point step sizes can silently drop or add one extra value right at the boundary — arange's exact count is worth checking, not assuming.
slides.teaching: Name the one common bug explicitly here: arange can silently drop the exact stop value depending on floating-point step size.

slides.title: np.linspace, defined
slides.definition: np.linspace(start, stop, n) builds evenly spaced values by COUNT. The stop value is INCLUDED — you say exactly how many points you want, both ends included.

example.head: np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9)
example.body: Gives exactly 9 values from 0.20 to 0.60, both ends included — the choice every sweep in this deck uses from here on, because both bounds are exactly the values worth checking.

slides.note: Prefer linspace when you know how many points you want; prefer arange when you know the exact step size between them.
slides.teaching: linspace's 'give me exactly n points, both ends included' is why today's sweeps all use linspace from here on — point back at arange's boundary bug as the reason.

slides.title: Sweep 1: wwr alone, shade_m held at the baseline 0.30
slides.code:
wwr_vals = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9)
e_wwr = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.30))

print(np.round(wwr_vals, 2))
print(np.round(e_wwr, 3))
print('range:', round(e_wwr.max() - e_wwr.min(), 3))
slides.explainHead: wwr alone swings the score by 28.4
slides.explainBody: linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9) makes 9 evenly spaced wwr values, both ends included. energy_proxy runs on all 9 at once. The score swings from about 24.7 down to -3.67 — a range of 28.373, with the best of these 9 near wwr=0.50.
slides.teaching: Ask students to name the best wwr value from this printout before revealing the range number — reinforces reading an array, not just admiring it.

slides.title: Sweep 2: shade_m alone, wwr held at the baseline 0.40
slides.code:
shade_vals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 9)
e_shade = energy_proxy((0.40, shade_vals))

print(np.round(shade_vals, 2))
print(np.round(e_shade, 3))
print('range:', round(e_shade.max() - e_shade.min(), 3))
slides.explainHead: shade_m alone barely moves the score
slides.explainBody: Same method, same nine-point sweep, this time on shade_m with wwr fixed at 0.40. The score barely moves — a range of only 3.46, a small fraction of wwr's 28.373.
slides.teaching: Let the obvious-looking conclusion form out loud: 'wwr matters, shade_m basically doesn't.' The next few slides exist to test that conclusion, not just state it.

slides.title: First read: wwr looks about 8x more important
slides.callout: Before trusting this: both numbers came from ONE fixed value of the OTHER variable. What if that fixed value happened to be a bad place to stand?
slides.teaching: Read the callout aloud before moving on — it is the exact question the next few slides answer, not a rhetorical aside.

slides.title: Wait — check it again from a different starting point
slides.statement: A one-at-a-time sweep only tells you about the one slice of the other variable you happened to fix.
slides.supporting: Re-run both sweeps, but this time fix each variable somewhere else — and see whether 'wwr matters, shade_m doesn't' still holds up.
slides.teaching: This is the trap slide. Do not resolve it yet — let the class sit with the possibility that the first read was incomplete before the next two slides reveal exactly how incomplete.

slides.title: Predict: does the trap survive a different baseline?
slides.code:
# same shade_m sweep, wwr fixed differently
shade_vals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 9)
e_shade2 = energy_proxy((0.28, shade_vals))
range2 = e_shade2.max() - e_shade2.min()
slides.question: Does shade_m stay flat at a different wwr?
options: No -- it jumps past wwr's own range of 28.373
Yes -- it stays near its original range of 3.46
No -- it grows some, to about 10, still under 28.373
No -- it shrinks even further, toward 0
slides.why: At wwr=0.28, shade_m's range jumps from 3.46 to 33.996 — past wwr's own 28.373. The first read was an artifact of the fixed baseline.
slides.teaching: Take the room's vote out loud before revealing — most will pick B, the exact overgeneralization the last two slides quietly set up.

slides.title: Same two sweeps, different fixed baselines
slides.code:
# shade_m swept, wwr now fixed at 0.28 instead of 0.40
e_shade2 = energy_proxy((0.28, shade_vals))
print('shade range @ wwr=0.28:',
      round(e_shade2.max() - e_shade2.min(), 3))

# wwr swept, shade_m now fixed at 0.90 instead of 0.30
e_wwr2 = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.90))
print('wwr range @ shade=0.90:',
      round(e_wwr2.max() - e_wwr2.min(), 3))
slides.output:
shade range @ wwr=0.28: 33.996
wwr range @ shade=0.90: 33.182
slides.explainHead: shade_m was never the less-important variable
slides.explainBody: Fixed at wwr=0.28 instead of 0.40, shade_m's own range jumps from 3.46 to 33.996 — bigger than wwr's original 28.373. The earlier conclusion was an artifact of WHERE the other variable happened to be fixed, not a fact about the formula.
slides.teaching: State plainly: this is not a trick question with a hidden gotcha unrelated to the real world — design teams make exactly this mistake when they test one variable at a time against whatever baseline they already had on the table.

slides.title: The lesson: one slice is never the whole answer

left.head: What went wrong
left.body: Each 1-D sweep only explored a single line through a two-variable space — like judging a whole floor plan from one hallway. Depending on which hallway (which fixed baseline) you picked, either variable can look unimportant.

right.head: What's needed instead
right.body: Evaluate EVERY combination of wwr and shade_m together, not one variable with the other frozen. That needs a tool that builds every (wwr, shade_m) pair from two separate swept lists at once.

slides.teaching: Do not name meshgrid yet on this slide — let the need for it land first as a plain-language requirement, then name the tool two slides from now.

slides.title: Boolean mask, defined
slides.definition: An array of True/False values, one per element, built from a comparison like scores <= 15. Applying the mask, scores[mask], keeps only the elements where the condition holds.

example.head: e_wwr <= 15.0
example.body: Compares every element of e_wwr to 15.0 at once, giving one True/False per position. wwr_vals[mask] then pulls out only the passing wwr values — 4 of the original 9 meet this target.

slides.note: Same idea as filtering a pandas Series with & / | in Week 5 — a mask here is the identical concept, one level closer to the raw array.
slides.teaching: Connect back to Week 5's Boolean filtering on a pandas Series (& / | on conditions) — this is the identical idea, one level closer to the raw array.

slides.title: Flag which wwr values meet a target of 15 or better
slides.code:
target = 15.0
meets_target = e_wwr <= target

print(meets_target)
print('passing wwr values:', wwr_vals[meets_target])
slides.output:
[False False False False False  True  True  True  True]
passing wwr values: [0.45 0.5  0.55 0.6 ]
slides.explainHead: A mask both flags AND filters
slides.explainBody: e_wwr <= target compares every element of e_wwr to 15.0 at once, producing one True/False per position — no loop. wwr_vals[meets_target] then uses that same mask to pull out only the wwr values that pass: 4 of the original 9 (0.45, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60) meet this target at shade_m=0.30.
slides.teaching: Point out the mask has the exact same shape (9,) as e_wwr and wwr_vals — that shape match is what lets one array's True/False values select from a different array.

slides.title: np.meshgrid, defined
slides.definition: Takes two separate 1-D arrays and builds two full 2-D grids so every combination of the two variables exists side by side, ready for one vectorized formula call.

example.head: x=[1,2,3], y=[10,20]
example.body: WW, SS = np.meshgrid(x, y) gives WW=[[1,2,3],[1,2,3]] and SS=[[10,10,10],[20,20,20]]. Row r, column c of WW and SS together name one of all 2x3=6 (x,y) pairs.

slides.note: meshgrid's first argument becomes the grid's COLUMNS, the second becomes its ROWS — that is why WW and SS both come back shaped (7, 9) for 9 wwr values and 7 shade_m values, not (9, 7).
slides.teaching: Walk the tiny example on the board before the real one — point at WW[0,1]=2 and SS[0,1]=10 together meaning the pair (2, 10), one of all 6 combinations.

slides.title: One meshgrid call, exploded

parts.label: Two grids come back
parts.body: One grid per swept variable, each already shaped to line up with the other.

parts.label: Meshgrid call
parts.body: Builds every (wwr, shade_m) combination from two separate 1-D arrays.

parts.label: Second 1-D array (7 values)
parts.body: Becomes each grid's ROWS — confirmed by the (7, 9) shape on the next slide.

slides.teaching: Point at each numbered chip in order and have students say, out loud, what shape WW and SS will come back in before the next slide confirms (7, 9).

slides.title: Sweep both variables together — every combination, one call
slides.code:
wwr_grid = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9)
shade_grid = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 7)
WW, SS = np.meshgrid(wwr_grid, shade_grid)

print('WW shape:', WW.shape)
Z = energy_proxy((WW, SS))
print('Z shape:', Z.shape)

best = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(Z), Z.shape)
print('coarse best so far:', WW[best], SS[best], round(Z[best], 3))
slides.output:
WW shape: (7, 9)
Z shape: (7, 9)
coarse best so far: 0.3 0.7999999999999999 -3.924
slides.explainBody: WW and SS both have shape (7, 9) — 63 (wwr, shade_m) pairs, every one of the 9 wwr values crossed with every one of the 7 shade_m values. energy_proxy((WW, SS)) evaluates every pair at once, no loop. np.argmin(Z) finds WHERE Z's smallest value sits, flattened into one long list; np.unravel_index turns that flat position back into a (row, column) pair, so WW[best]/SS[best] read the actual wwr/shade_m. This coarse grid already points to the right NEIGHBORHOOD — low wwr, high shade_m.
slides.teaching: Name the count explicitly: 9x7=63 calls done in one vectorized line, versus 63 typed lines the naive way — and this is still a coarse grid, about to get much finer.

slides.title: Read the surface: both basins, one clearly better
slides.explainBody: Every one of the 63 grid points from the previous slide, colored by score tier — axes shown as percent and centimeters so every tick reads as a plain number (e.g. x=50 means wwr=0.50; y=90 means shade_m=0.90 m). The lowest-score points cluster in TWO separate places — lower-left (low wwr, high shade_m) and lower-right (mid-high wwr, low shade_m) — exactly the two basins this fictional formula was built with. The next two slides name how much better one is.
slides.teaching: Have students point, before the next slide, at which of the two clusters they would bet is the better one and why — no wrong answer yet, just a prediction to check.

slides.title: Predict: which basin actually wins, and by how much?
slides.code:
wwr_fine = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 81)
shade_fine = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 61)
WWf, SSf = np.meshgrid(wwr_fine, shade_fine)
Zf = energy_proxy((WWf, SSf))
best = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(Zf), Zf.shape)
slides.question: Which basin wins on the fine 81x61 grid, and by how much?
options: Lower-left (low wwr, high shade): about -11.1, beats the other by about 4
Lower-right (higher wwr, low shade): about -7.1, beats the other by about 4
Both basins are tied within rounding error
slides.why: The 81x61 grid (4,941 points, verified) finds its best sampled point at (0.275, 0.900) = -11.135 — beating the other basin's -7.08 by 4.06.
slides.teaching: Have students commit to a letter before revealing — the coarse 63-point grid from the previous slide already hinted at the lower-left region without confirming the margin.

slides.title: A more precise sampled answer from a finer sweep
slides.callout: An 81×61 grid checks 4,941 sampled combinations and finds -11.135 at (0.275, 0.900). Points between grid nodes remain unchecked, so report this as the best sampled point, not a proof of the continuous global optimum.
slides.teaching: Name explicitly: this is the exact same meshgrid technique from a few slides ago, just with far more points in each linspace call — no new tool, only finer resolution. State that this fine grid is a real, previously verified computation, not an estimate.

slides.title: Read the sensitivity result
slides.prompt: Using the table above, answer in one sentence: which region should Radley Hall's design team target, and by how much does it beat the runner-up?
steps: Name the (wwr, shade_m) pair with the lowest energy_proxy.
State the numeric gap between the two regions (-11.135 vs. -7.08).
State the improvement over the 22.076 baseline design.
Write one sentence a design team could act on -- region, direction, and size of the gain.
slides.teaching: Expected sentence shape: 'Move toward low wwr (~0.28) and deep shading (~0.90 m); this beats the other low region by about 4 points and the current baseline by about 33 points.' Reject any answer naming wwr or shade_m alone as 'the important variable' — today's whole point is that the pair, not either alone, decides it.

slides.title: Transfer the sweep: insulation thickness × glazing ratio
slides.prompt: Test every combination of insulation thickness and glazing ratio against a simplified energy-and-daylight proxy.
steps: Choose defensible ranges and units for both parameters before generating values.
Use meshgrid so every thickness–glazing pair is evaluated.
Mask combinations that fail a stated daylight or constructability threshold.
Identify a promising region—not one magic point—and state one proxy limitation.
slides.teaching: Assess the workflow, not a prescribed optimum: range → meshgrid → vectorized evaluation → feasibility mask → region interpretation. The transfer makes clear that a 2-D sweep reveals interactions hidden by one-at-a-time slices. Accept limitations such as simplified envelope geometry, assumed climate, omitted cost, discrete product sizes, or proxy validity.

slides.title: The sweep-and-read pipeline, in order

steps.label: POSE
steps.head: State the question first
steps.body: Which variable, or combination, moves the outcome most — before any array syntax.

steps.label: SWEEP
steps.head: linspace, then vectorize
steps.body: Generate values with linspace; call the formula on the whole ndarray, not in a loop.

steps.label: COMBINE
steps.head: meshgrid + mask
steps.body: meshgrid pairs both variables together; a boolean mask flags which pairs meet a target.

steps.label: READ
steps.head: State the finding
steps.body: Name the best region and the size of the gain — in one sentence a design team could use.

slides.teaching: This four-step order is what Wednesday's studio repeats end to end on the exact same formula — point at this slide again before that session starts.

slides.title: Milestone: Project 2 opens today
slides.statement: Project 2 — Predict, Optimize, Decide — is assigned this week: the problem-area, dataset, and prediction/optimization pairing window opens now, with more runway than any other project milestone this semester.
slides.supporting: Today's two-variable sweep is the exact kind of Part I evidence Project 2 requires on your own formulation. Wednesday's studio builds the graded artifact; this lecture slide is not graded again.
slides.teaching: State plainly: dataset/problem-area selection for Project 2 opens now, running through Week 10's linprog studio. Point back at today's sweep-and-read pipeline slide as literally the Part I sensitivity-check requirement students will repeat on their own problem in a few weeks.

slides.title: The question comes first; the tools answer it
takeaways: A one-at-a-time sweep can give a confidently wrong answer -- it only reports the one slice of the other variable you fixed.
ndarray plus linspace lets one line evaluate many designs at once; a boolean mask flags which ones meet a target.
meshgrid combines two swept variables into every real combination -- the only way to compare them fairly.
The verified answer here: aim near wwr=0.275, shade_m=0.90 -- about 33 points better than baseline, and clearly better than the other low region.
slides.teaching: Exit prompt: ask students to restate, from memory and without notes, why the first 1-D sweep's conclusion (wwr matters, shade_m doesn't) turned out to be incomplete rather than wrong-on-its-face.
